content: To achieve the necessary quantitative and qualitative improvements in health professional education, it is essential to align training outputs with the objectives outlined in the Human Resources for Health (HRH) plan, while operating within the constraints of available resources. The implementation of transformative changes in health professional education must be guided by clear objectives. These include ensuring the availability of a workforce that is adequate in both numbers and skill mix, and that possesses the competencies and professional outlook required to meet the needs of the population it serves. To monitor the progress and effectiveness of these changes, mechanisms must be established to track outcomes and provide timely feedback to policymakers. This allows for the adaptation of policies as needed. Valid and updated information must be made available in an accessible and interpretable format to support this process. Monitoring and evaluation are critical components of implementing change, but they often present challenges. Leaders responsible for transforming health workforce education must address key policy issues, such as determining what to monitor, how to monitor it, who should be responsible, and how to ensure that the information generated is effectively utilized. Monitoring should not be an end in itself. The value of monitoring lies in its ability to inform decision-making. Not all information carries equal weight or influence on decisions, so it is crucial for policymakers and implementers to identify their specific information needs. Monitoring everything indiscriminately can lead to the accumulation of unused data. Instead, the focus should be on identifying critical data and information that are essential for decision-making, whether for adjusting interventions to changing circumstances (formative evaluation) or for deciding whether to continue or discontinue implementation (summative evaluation). Typically, information is required on the inputs, processes, and results of interventions. Among these, results are often the most challenging to measure, as they take time to manifest. The World Health Organization (WHO) Handbook on monitoring and evaluation of human resources for health suggests focusing on seven dimensions when monitoring entry into the health labor market, four of which pertain to education: (i) the pool of eligible candidates for health education and training, (ii) recruitment and selection of students, (iii) accreditation of education and training institutions, and (iv) the capacity and output of these institutions. It is also important to consider the subsequent employment of graduates. Producing educated health professionals without ensuring job opportunities is counterproductive. This framework can serve as a starting point for defining what is worth monitoring. Indicators can be developed for each dimension to provide the necessary information for effective monitoring of implementation processes and outcomes. Effective monitoring requires robust information systems that produce relevant and reliable data in a timely and accessible manner. However, in many countries, basic health workforce data, including those related to education processes, are often incomplete. Data are typically scattered across various organizations, each collecting information on different parameters using different definitions and timeframes. This results in inconsistencies in data quality, validity, reliability, comprehensiveness, and comparability over time. In general, data on health professionals employed in public services are more complete than those in the private sector. Few countries produce data on multiple employment, productivity, or the mobility of health workers. The introduction of transformative changes in education provides an opportunity to review the strengths and weaknesses of current information systems and to build systems capable of monitoring and assessing the effects of changes on the quantity, quality, and relevance of new health professionals. To interpret data and evaluate policy implications, explicit criteria and targets for expected results are needed. These may include training institutions (for quantity), professional regulatory bodies such as accreditation agencies and professional councils (for quality and relevance), and employers (for quantity, quality, and relevance). High levels of collaboration among key stakeholders are necessary to agree on the data to be collected, the definition of indicators, and the sharing of results. A centralized clearinghouse that gathers data from various sources may be required. This could take the form of an independent public institute, a health workforce observatory, or another type of organization. Its goal should be to ensure the quality and relevance of data, enabling the tracking of graduates, particularly their professional choices, such as their field and location of practice. A major challenge is ensuring that the information reaches those who can best use it for policy and decision-making purposes and that it is properly interpreted and utilized. Policy decisions are not based solely on evidence, but valid data can be a critical input. Some countries have demonstrated effective ways to bridge the gap between data collection, analysis, and decision-making. Leaders of change in education can learn from the experiences of organizations such as the Canadian Health Services Foundation, the Health Foundation in England, and the Center for Advancing Health in the USA, which have shown that knowledge brokering and exchange can be systematically carried out. Lower-income countries may not be able to afford the investments made in Canada, the United Kingdom, or the USA, but low-cost actions are feasible. Failing to inform decisions can ultimately be more costly. Transforming health professional education is not merely a technical exercise; it is a highly political process that occurs in a complex environment, affecting the values, objectives, power, and interests of numerous stakeholders. A new model for health professional education requires significant cultural and organizational changes, as well as substantial new investments. This transformation demands a strategic approach to scaling up, including clear definitions of expected results, the actions needed to achieve them, how they will be implemented, and the resources required. A plan is useful but insufficient on its own. Stakeholders must commit to its implementation, resources must be mobilized, and political support must be maintained. Leadership and good governance are critical to progress in education reform, which is often fraught with obstacles. Leaders must understand the multiple dimensions and interconnections of the components of transformation and scaling up, as well as the complex relationships among various stakeholders. Governance must also be adjusted, encompassing the formal and informal rules and norms that define roles, responsibilities, and decision-making mechanisms in a given sector. Good governance results from a combination of institutional and organizational mechanisms that support change, along with the technical and political capacity and will to implement change. In many cases, governance related to the health workforce is concentrated in ministries of health, where capacity is often weak, as seen in sub-Saharan Africa, which has the highest number of countries experiencing a human resources crisis. Poor governance leads to inefficiency, politically motivated decisions, lack of transparency and accountability, and corruption. Smart governance in health has been defined as governing through collaboration, engaging citizens and stakeholders, mixing regulation and persuasion, utilizing independent agencies and expert bodies, and employing adaptive policies, resilient structures, and foresight. This approach represents a significant departure from top-down, centralized governance based on coercion. It requires leaders who understand change, believe in it, and can engage others effectively.
